why_how.text: You enter an interstate by an entrance ramp, paying careful attention to the signs because an exit ramp marked do not enter and wrong way often sits next to the entrance ramp, and advisory speed signs appear on ramps that curve sharply.

About halfway along the entrance ramp check the interstate traffic with quick glances over your shoulder and to the side, watch the vehicles ahead of you entering the acceleration lane, use your turn signal, and look for a gap in approaching traffic while adjusting your speed to meet it.
As you merge make sure you are traveling at the same speed as the other traffic, and do not cut sharply to the left into the traffic stream but follow the lane, merge, and only then change lanes.
If another vehicle is ahead of you in the acceleration lane be prepared for it to slow or stop without warning, and do not stop on the ramp or in the acceleration lane.

If no gap in traffic is available it may be necessary to drive onto the shoulder beyond the end of the acceleration lane and stop, but because entering the traffic stream from a stop is hazardous this maneuver is a last resort.
Traffic already on the interstate has the right-of-way, and you cannot count on other drivers seeing you or moving over to give you room to enter.

When exiting an interstate watch for the signs that show where your exit is and which lane to use, then signal and move into that lane well before the exit, because changing lanes at the last moment risks missing the exit or causing a crash.

Most interstate exits have a deceleration lane for slowing before the exit ramp, so never slow down on the interstate itself but wait until you are in the deceleration lane and brake gently until your speed matches the posted exit ramp limit.
Braking for an exit belongs in the deceleration lane, never on the interstate itself, and the target is the posted exit ramp speed.
When no gap appears, the last-resort stop is on the shoulder beyond the end of the acceleration lane, never on the ramp or in the acceleration lane itself.

Traffic already on the interstate holds the right-of-way over entering traffic, so the entering driver matches speed, merges within the lane and only afterwards changes lanes rather than cutting sharply left.

why_how.text: Interstate and divided highways have largely removed the chance of head-on collisions, but interstate driving is very different and demands complete awareness of high-speed driving and constant alertness.

Trucks and buses entering an interstate may need extra time to adjust to the traffic pattern, so give them extra time and space, and slower traffic should drive in the right-hand lane except when passing.
Interstate shoulders are only for disabled vehicles and must not be used for changing drivers, reading a map or other non-emergency purposes, which belong in a rest area or off the interstate.
Do not stop in an exit gore, the triangular area between the through lane and the exit ramp, because a driver who missed the exit may try to cross the gore and strike your vehicle.
No parking is permitted on the shoulders of interstates, and parked vehicles may be towed.

Never drive faster than the legal speed limit, do not drive slower than fifty-five miles per hour on an interstate unless weather or road conditions are bad or a lower speed is posted, and always drive at a steady speed.

Driving much slower than other interstate drivers creates a hazard because others may be forced to change lanes abruptly, so always drive in the right-hand lane unless you are passing another vehicle.

State law requires headlights to be turned on during adverse conditions, and in such conditions you should adjust your driving, keep an adequate following distance and adjust your speed to allow a safe stop.
The interstate floor is fifty-five miles per hour unless conditions are bad or a lower speed is posted, the ceiling is always the legal limit, and the right lane is the place to be unless passing.
The shoulder is for disabled vehicles only and never for parking, while the exit gore between the through lane and the ramp is a place never to stop at all.

why_how.text: Interstate highways are identified by distinctive red, white and blue shields, even-numbered interstates run east to west, and odd-numbered interstates run north to south.
A three-digit interstate number whose first digit is even identifies a beltway or bypass around a city, while a three-digit number whose first digit is odd identifies a spur route.

Because interstate entrances and exits can be far apart, plan your route in advance and check gas, water, oil and tires including the spare before leaving, since a breakdown on an interstate costs time and can be dangerous.

On an interstate the first guide sign for an interchange is placed well before the point where you must turn off, giving time to change lanes and exit smoothly, so watch the guide signs to avoid hazardous last-minute maneuvers.

Where the number of through lanes changes, an added lane is usually obvious, while a removed lane usually ends at a fork or exit and is indicated by a black and yellow panel below the green and white overhead guide sign.

An interchange is the intersection of two highways at different levels, over and under, with separate connecting roads that let vehicles cross, enter or leave either road without interfering with others, and the three most common types are cloverleaf, diamond and trumpet.
An even interstate number means an east-west route while an odd number means a north-south route.
A three-digit interstate number starting with an even digit is a beltway or bypass around a city, while one starting with an odd digit is a spur route.
A removed through lane is announced by a black and yellow panel beneath the green and white overhead guide sign, whereas an added lane is usually obvious without one.
Cloverleaf, diamond and trumpet are the three common interchange types, and every interchange joins two highways at different levels with connecting roads.

why_how.text: West Virginia law reserves designated parking spaces for mobility impaired citizens whose condition limits their ability to walk reasonable distances, and people who routinely transport mobility impaired persons may also use those spaces.

To obtain a mobility impaired parking placard or license plate a doctor must certify the condition on a form the DMV provides, the DMV issues the placard or plate after approving the application, and the mobility impaired license plate carries a transfer fee of ten dollars and fifty cents.
It is illegal to park a vehicle in a designated mobility impaired area unless it displays a mobility impaired parking placard or license plate.

About one in every ten people has some disability, no single set of rules can judge every person's ability to drive safely, and an applicant with a physical disability or medical problem that may interfere with driving should prepare a letter explaining the situation to accompany the license application.

A driver who needs adaptive aids such as hand controls can get a list of manufacturers from the driver's license examiner or from the Driver Education Department of the West Virginia Division of Rehabilitation Services.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act the DMV does not discriminate on the basis of disability, generally provides aids and services for effective communication on request, makes reasonable modifications to its policies, and welcomes service animals in its offices even where pets are prohibited.
Anyone who needs an auxiliary aid or a modification of DMV procedures should contact the DMV no later than forty-eight hours before the scheduled arrival.

The Americans with Disabilities Act does not require the DMV to fundamentally alter its programs or take on an undue financial or administrative burden, and the DMV will not place a surcharge on a person or group with disabilities to cover the cost of aids, services or modifications.

Questions or concerns about accessibility go to the DMV's ADA coordinator, and reasonable modifications include retrieving items from public locations that are not accessible to people who use wheelchairs.

A mobility impaired placard or plate requires a doctor's certification on the DMV form and the plate carries a ten dollar and fifty cent transfer fee, and parking in a designated space without displaying one is illegal.
An accommodation request to the DMV must arrive at least forty-eight hours before the visit, and the DMV may not charge the person with a disability for the aid or modification.
